strengths: Addresses a relevant and timely question: how to extend effective context for transformer-based offline RL policies beyond the ~30-step context used by Decision Transformer.

The adaptation of RMT-style read/write memory tokens to the (return, state, action) token structure of DT is described clearly, including the segment-wise training procedure with detached memory and gradient flow across segments (Figures 2-4).
Includes a useful controlled baseline (DT-XL: identical architecture/segment training without memory tokens) that isolates the contribution of the memory tokens themselves.

Ablations over number of segments, memory size, segment overlap, and memory fixation are provided; the segment-overlap/memory-fixation ablation on MuJoCo (Table 3) is informative and shows a large effect.
Attention-map analyses attempt to give interpretable evidence that memory tokens are read and written as intended, with consistency across layers, segments, and both domains.
Code and weights are stated to be publicly released, and hyperparameters are documented.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a direct application of Recurrent Memory Transformer memory tokens (plus Transformer-XL hidden-state carryover) to Decision Transformer, with no new algorithmic insight specific to RL (e.g., handling of return conditioning, credit assignment, or partial observability).

The central claim that the model is 'significantly superior' is not statistically supported. On Atari, RMDT vs DT-XL overlaps heavily within reported standard deviations (e.g., Qbert 12800±1120 vs 12300±1530; Pong 17.1±0.94 vs 16.6±0.99; Breakout 123.8±35.6 vs 99.6±29.8). Only 3 seeds x 10 episodes, no significance tests or confidence intervals.

Much of the Atari gain appears attributable to segment-wise training rather than memory: DT-XL already recovers most of the improvement over DT on Qbert and Pong, weakening the paper's headline conclusion.

MuJoCo results show essentially no benefit: mean 75.2 vs DT 74.7 and CQL 77.6, with very large standard deviations (e.g., ±14.4, ±18.9, ±16.1) and clear regressions on Walker2d medium-expert and both HalfCheetah/Hopper medium-replay. The paper nonetheless claims superiority over TAP in the conclusion, which is not supported.

No evaluation on benchmarks that actually require long-term memory (e.g., POPGym, Memory Maze, T-Maze/passive recall tasks, Memory Gym, or partially observable variants). Atari with frame stacking and MuJoCo are near-Markovian, so the paper cannot demonstrate the capability it claims to add; the limitation section acknowledges this but does not address it.

Missing comparisons to closely related memory/long-context DT variants and stronger offline RL baselines (e.g., Online DT, Q-learning DT, Multi-Game DT, Agent Transformer variants, GTrXL, or contemporaneous memory-augmented DT work). Only 4 Atari games are used, citing compute limits.
No analysis of computational cost, memory footprint, or wall-clock/inference overhead, despite the motivation being the quadratic cost of attention.

Interpretability claims are weak: attention maps of a single randomly chosen head with qualitative descriptions ('bright stripes') are not evidence that memory encodes task-relevant information; no causal probing (e.g., memory ablation/shuffling at inference, information-retrieval probes).

Presentation issues undermine the quality: typos throughout ('MoJoko', 'Transformative models'), duplicated references [8] and [9], a miscited claim (Transformer-XL effective 1M-token context attributed to Deformable DETR [22]), placeholder text for the code repository link, and figure captions repeated verbatim (Figures 9 and 10).

Several methodological details are unclear: how memory is handled at evaluation/rollout time in Atari, why memory is described as inserted only at 'the beginning and end of the first segment', how return-to-go is conditioned across segments, and how the 25% overlap interacts with the reported 150-frame effective context.
